title: 道德經 第四十一章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 41, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 73. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 41 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 同異 (Sameness and Difference). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
上士聞道，
勤而行之；

morph.gloss: the upper, the topmost of a set
a man of standing — the knight-officer class, and so anyone who has a calling and is good at it
to hear, to catch a sound (the result; 聽 tīng is the listening that may or may not achieve it)
to toil, to wear oneself out at a thing
and then, and so (links one predicate to the next)
to walk; here to put into practice, to carry out
it — the object pronoun, standing for the Way, not the genitive 'of'

sentences.l:
The upper man of standing hears the Way,
toils and puts it into practice;
sentences.i: When the best sort of man hears the Way, he labours to put it into practice;
sentences.n:
士 is one of the book's few social words. It named the lowest rank of the old nobility — the man who bore arms and held office — and by Laozi's day it had widened into something like 'a man of standing, one who has a calling'. 上士, 中士 and 下士 were also three actual grades of Zhou office, so the three-rung ladder this chapter opens with is borrowed from a real table of ranks and used as a scale of understanding.

而 again, and here it is plain sequence rather than 'and yet' — he toils, and he walks it. Only the sense of the two halves ever tells you which.

行 is literally 'to walk'. A way is a road, so what you do with it is walk it; 行道 is 'to practise the Way' by the same figure that gives English 'to follow' a teaching.

sentences.t:
中士聞道，
若存若亡；
下士聞道，
大笑之。
不笑不足以為道。
故建言有之﹕

morph.gloss: the middle, the middling one of a set
a man of standing — the knight-officer class, and so anyone who has a calling and is good at it
to hear, to catch a sound (the result; 聽 tīng is the listening that may or may not achieve it)
as if, seeming — it is like
to be there, to persist, to be kept in being
to be gone, to have perished, to be lost
the lower, the bottom of a set
a man of standing — the knight-officer class, and so anyone who has a calling and is good at it
to hear, to catch a sound (the result; 聽 tīng is the listening that may or may not achieve it)
great, greatly — here adverbial, before the verb
it — object pronoun again, the Way
to be laughed at — the same verb, read passively because it has no object
wéi: to be, to count as, to be taken for
the set sayings — established maxims; possibly the title of a lost collection the chapter is quoting from
to set up, to establish, to plant upright
this — the object pronoun pointing forward at the twelve lines that follow

sentences.l:
The middling man of standing hears the Way —
as if it were there, as if it were gone;
the lower man of standing hears the Way —
he laughs aloud at it.
Not laughed at, it would not be enough to count as the Way.
And so the set sayings have this:
sentences.i: When the middling sort hears the Way, he half keeps it and half lets it slip; when the low sort hears the Way, he laughs out loud. If it drew no laughter, it would not amount to the Way. And so the old maxims run:
sentences.n:
若存若亡 is a shape the language uses often: 若 twice, once over each of two opposites, to say that a thing will not settle into either. 存 is 'be there, be kept in being', 亡 is 'be gone'; the man half has the Way and half has lost it, and the line does not say which moment you would catch him in.

不笑不足以為道 has no 'if' in it, and no 'would'. Classical Chinese sets down two predicates and leaves the hinge between them to the reader; English cannot, so a conditional has to be supplied. Notice also that the first 笑 has no object and so reads passively — 'not laughed at'. Nothing in the writing marks that. Position does it all.

The argument in that line is not a joke about fools. It is a test: a Way that the coarse understanding could take in would be a Way cut to the size of coarse understanding. The laughter is evidence. Chapter 78 closes with the same thought put flat — 正言若反, 'straight words seem the reverse of themselves' — and that sentence is the key to everything the twelve maxims below are doing.

建言 is read here as a noun, 'the established sayings', and the twelve short lines that follow are the quotation (four characters each, but for 廣德若不足). Whether it is a general phrase or the actual name of a lost book of maxims is not decidable from the text, and both have been held.

morph.gloss: dark, dim, hard to make out

sentences.l: The bright way, as if dark;
sentences.i: The way that gives light seems dim;
sentences.n:
Twelve maxims follow, and the first eight are built on one frame: a thing named, then 若 'as if', then that thing's own opposite. There is no verb 'to be' anywhere in them — 若 is the only verb each line has, and it carries the whole weight. The last four change the frame; the note at 大方無隅 says how.

明 and 昧 are already a pair in this book: chapter 14 said of the Way that 其上不皦，其下不昧, its top is not dazzling and its underside not dim. Here the two are stacked in one line, which is a sharper way of saying the same thing.

morph.gloss: to withdraw, to step back, to retire from the scene

sentences.l: The advancing way, as if retreating;
sentences.i: The way that goes forward seems to fall back;

morph.gloss: level, smooth, with nothing raised for the eye or the foot to catch
a knot or slub in a silk thread, and so a flaw, a roughness — a rare character

sentences.l: The level way, as if knotted;
sentences.i: The way that runs smooth seems full of snags;
sentences.n:
夷 is the word chapter 14 gave a name to: 視之不見名曰夷, 'look at it and do not see it — its name is called the Featureless'. Level, with nothing standing up to be seen. 纇 is its exact opposite drawn from the loom: the lump in a silk thread that catches the shuttle. It is a rare character, met almost nowhere else, and its sense here is secure from the contrast even where it would not be secure on its own.

Hear these three lines together: 昧 mèi, 退 tuì, 纇 lèi. On the standard groupings of Old Chinese rhyme these three belong to one group, and unusually for this book enough of it has come through that a modern reading still chimes — the endings are not identical in Mandarin, but they answer one another. This is verse, and here you can nearly hear that it is.

morph.gloss: potency — the power a thing has by simply being what it is
a valley, the empty low place everything runs down into

sentences.l: The highest potency, as if a valley;
sentences.n: 上德 is the term chapter 38 opened with — 上德不德, the highest potency does not make a show of potency. The valley is one of this book's fixed images and always carries the same argument: it is low, so things come to it; it is empty, so there is room. Chapters 6, 15, 28 and 39 all use it. Note that it is being offered here as a *defect* — the point of the list is that the genuine article looks like the lack of it.

morph.gloss: here 'soiled, stained' — the concrete reading commentators take in this line; the character's ordinary classical sense is 'disgrace'

sentences.i: What is purest white seems stained;
sentences.n: 辱 in this book has meant disgrace — chapter 13's 寵辱若驚, favour and disgrace alike a shock. Set against 白 'white' it has to be read concretely here, a thing dirtied — that is the commentators' reading, and it is a reading, not a settled fact about the character. The pairing is not invented for this line; chapter 28 set 白 against 黑 and 榮 against 辱 within a few characters of each other, so both readings of 辱 are live in the same neighbourhood and the line trades on it.

sentences.l: Broad potency, as if not enough;
sentences.i: Potency that reaches wide seems to fall short;
sentences.n: 不足 appeared six lines ago in 不足以為道, where it meant 'not fit to be'. Here the same two characters are praise. Nothing distinguishes them but what they sit next to; this is the ordinary condition of reading Classical Chinese rather than a trick of this passage.

morph.gloss: to set up, to plant firmly upright
slack, perfunctory, done by halves — the classical sense. It is NOT the modern Mandarin 'to steal'

sentences.n:
偷 is one of the sharper false friends in the book. In modern Chinese it is 'to steal'; classically it is 苟且 — slack, careless, doing a thing anyhow and letting it go at that. Taking it as 'thievish' here makes a line that does not answer 建, 'planted firmly', which is what 若 requires it to answer.

建 also picks up 建言 from the introduction — the sayings were 'set up' by the same verb that here sets up potency.

morph.gloss: substance, the plain stuff a thing is made of, before any polish
genuine, not counterfeit; true to what the thing actually is
to change, to alter — properly of a dye losing its colour

sentences.l: Substance genuine, as if it faded;
sentences.i: What is genuine through and through seems to change colour;
sentences.n:
渝 is a dyer's word: the colour that will not hold. Against 真, 'the real thing', it makes the same shape as the eight lines before it.

These five maxims rhyme too, though less audibly to a modern ear: 谷 gǔ, 辱 rǔ, 足 zú, 偷 tōu, 渝 yú, and 隅 yú in the next line belong to one Old Chinese rhyme group. Mandarin has kept part of it — 谷, 辱 and 足 still chime, and 渝 with 隅 — and lost the join between the two halves.

morph.gloss: a square; and so a region, a quarter of the world
a corner, the angle where two sides of a square meet

sentences.l: A great square has no corners;
sentences.n:
The frame changes here: the last four maxims drop 若 and simply predicate. What they say is no longer 'looks like its opposite' but 'is, at the limit, without the thing that defines it'.

A square is known by its corners, so a square large enough has none you could stand at. 方 means the figure, and by extension a region or a quarter of the earth — the old cosmology made the earth square and the heavens round — so the line can also be heard as 'the great region has no boundary'. Both are available and neither cancels the other.

morph.gloss: a vessel, an implement — anything shaped so as to be used
to be completed, to be brought to fulfilment

sentences.l: A great vessel is late completed;
sentences.i: The great vessel is finished late;
sentences.n:
This is the one line of the chapter every Chinese speaker knows, and it has drifted: as a modern proverb 大器晚成 means that great talents mature slowly, which is encouragement. In the list it is doing what its neighbours do — the great vessel is not finished, as the great square has no corner.

The Mawangdui silk manuscripts do not read 晚 here. They have 免成, which on the usual reading is 'the great vessel is never completed' — 免 'to be exempt from, to avoid'. That fits the four lines around it exactly, all of which deny the defining feature outright, and many now think it the older reading. The received text has 晚, and 晚 is what stands here, with the manuscript on the record.

morph.gloss: a note, a shaped musical tone — as against 聲, the bare sound
so rare as to be barely there; of a sound, too faint to be heard

sentences.l: The great tone, faint of sound;
sentences.i: The great tone is barely a sound;
sentences.n:
希 is another word chapter 14 named: 聽之不聞名曰希, 'listen for it and do not hear it — its name is called the Faint'. So the line is not merely saying that the great music is quiet; it is calling it by the Way's own name.

音 and 聲 are not synonyms and the line depends on their not being. 聲 is sound as such, noise; 音 is sound formed into a note. Chapter 2 already paired them — 音聲相和, note and noise chime together.

morph.gloss: the Great Image — the Way considered as the one image behind all images; Wang Bi calls it the mother of the images of heaven
shape, outline — a thing's visible form

sentences.l: The Great Image has no shape;
sentences.n:
大象 is treated as one word because the book coins it: chapter 35 opened 執大象，天下往, 'hold fast the Great Image and all under heaven comes to you'. The three lines before it keep the same 大 X frame without being terms, which is why 大方, 大器 and 大音 stay as two words each.

象 is the character for an elephant, and how it came to mean 'image' is disputed — the old explanation, that the men of the Yellow River plain knew the elephant only from its bones and had to picture it, is a good story of uncertain standing. Whatever the history, 象 is 'likeness' throughout this book.

Now the rhyme: 成 chéng, 聲 shēng, 形 xíng, and 名 míng in the line to come. One Old Chinese rhyme group, and all four still chime in Mandarin. The twelve maxims are rhymed in three runs, and this is the last of them.

sentences.t:
道隱無名。
夫唯道，
善貸且成。

morph.gloss: hidden, withdrawn out of sight; to keep hidden
fú: now, as for — the particle that opens a general statement
it is only, it is precisely
good at, apt at (a verb taking what follows)
to lend, to give out on loan; to grant, to bestow

sentences.l:
The Way hides, and is without a name.
It is only the Way
that is good at lending, and at bringing to completion.
sentences.i: The Way keeps out of sight and has no name; and it is the Way alone that is good at giving out what things need and at bringing them to their fulfilment.
sentences.n:
夫唯 opens the book's clinching sentences. Usually a 故 or 是以 clause follows and the sense is causal, 'it is just because X that Y' — so in chapters 2, 8, 15 and 22. Here there is no second clause, and 唯 does its other job, the restrictive one: not 'because the Way' but 'the Way and nothing else'. Same two characters, and only the shape of the sentence after them tells you which.

貸 is the ordinary word for lending at interest, and it is startling here. What the Way gives out it does not give away: the things of the world hold their potency on loan and go on being what they are without ever owning it. Chapter 34's 衣養萬物而不為主 — it clothes and feeds the ten thousand things and does not make itself their master — says the same in more words.

The Mawangdui manuscripts read 善始且善成 here, 'good at beginning and good at completing', which turns the line into a plain pair and loses the loan. 貸 and 始 are not close in sound or shape, so this is a real difference between the witnesses rather than a slip, and which is older is not settled. The received reading is what stands.
